name: Elasticity
summary: The ability to scale capacity up and down automatically as demand changes, so you pay for what you use and idle resources shrink to near zero.
description: Elasticity is scalability that runs in both directions and on its own. An elastic architecture grows compute when a workload spikes and releases it when demand falls, ideally to zero when idle. It depends on separating storage from compute, serverless or autoscaled runtimes, and fast provisioning. Fixed on-prem clusters and always-on infrastructure are the opposite: they can be large, but they cannot cheaply shrink, so they trade elasticity for predictability.

mechanisms.name: Serverless compute
mechanisms.note: Query and job runtimes that provision on demand and bill per query or per second eliminate idle capacity entirely.

mechanisms.name: Warehouse auto-suspend and auto-resume
mechanisms.note: Compute clusters that pause when idle and resume on the next query shrink cost to zero between workloads.

mechanisms.name: Separation of storage and compute
mechanisms.note: Decoupling durable storage from transient compute lets compute scale to zero without losing data.

mechanisms.name: Kubernetes autoscaling
mechanisms.note: Horizontal pod and cluster autoscalers add and remove workers in response to queue depth or CPU pressure.

mechanisms.name: Consumer and partition autoscaling
mechanisms.note: Elastic stream platforms grow and shrink broker and consumer capacity to track fluctuating event rates.

manifestations.statement: Cloud warehouses auto-suspend between dbt runs and resume per query, so compute cost tracks actual transformation and query demand closely.
In-process DuckDB spins up only for the duration of a query and consumes nothing when idle, giving near-perfect elasticity at small scale.
Serving clusters can add replicas under load, but low-latency OLAP engines usually keep hot data resident and cannot fully scale to zero.
Job clusters spin up per pipeline run and terminate on completion, so batch compute is fully elastic against durable object-storage tables.
Data lives once in object storage while ephemeral engines start and stop per workload, giving strong elasticity across independent compute.
Embedding and retrieval jobs scale elastically, but always-on vector serving and LLM endpoints keep a baseline of non-elastic capacity.
Scheduled batch windows let compute spin up and release on a cadence, but fixed nightly clusters often stay provisioned longer than needed.
Streaming operators can autoscale, but stateful jobs must keep workers running continuously, so idle-time savings are limited.
Ingest and query tiers autoscale with traffic, yet continuous event flow means the platform rarely idles down to zero.
Customer-facing query load is spiky and elastic per tenant, but SLA guarantees push teams to keep warm capacity that erodes elasticity.
Device fleets emit a steady baseline stream around the clock, so ingest and storage capacity must stay provisioned and cannot shrink much.
On-prem hardware is a fixed capital cost that cannot scale down, so the on-prem half of the architecture is inherently inelastic.
The normalized enterprise core favors a stable, always-available integrated store, deliberately trading elasticity for consistency and governance.
Stateless event consumers autoscale well on Kubernetes, but the shared broker backbone stays continuously provisioned as a baseline cost.
Heavy always-on load pipelines and audit retention keep infrastructure resident, limiting how far the architecture can idle down.
Serving infrastructure can scale out as tenants and concurrency grow, but customer-facing SLAs favor provisioned headroom over aggressive scale-to-zero elasticity.

tradeoffs.title: Cost efficiency
tradeoffs.note: Autoscaling routinely overshoots demand, keeps idle headroom for safety, and pays cold-start and warm-pool waste, so elastic capacity is rarely as cost-optimal as steady-state provisioning.

tradeoffs.title: Latency
tradeoffs.note: Cold starts and scale-up lag mean new capacity is not instantly ready, so requests arriving during a demand spike see elevated latency until the system catches up.

tradeoffs.title: Operational complexity
tradeoffs.note: Getting elasticity right demands carefully tuned autoscaling policies, thresholds, cooldowns, and warm pools that are easy to misconfigure into flapping or under-provisioning.

tradeoffs.title: Consistency
tradeoffs.note: Scaling stateful services or stream operators mid-flight requires redistributing state and repartitioning keys, which is hard to do without dropping ordering or exactly-once guarantees.
